html:
In 2010 scientists published the complete genome of the apple. It confirmed that the wild apple of the Tian Shan mountains of Central Asia, Malus sieversii, is the main ancestor of the apples we eat.

Wild apple forests still grow on the slopes around Almaty in Kazakhstan, whose old name Alma-Ata is often read as "father of apples". The trees vary a lot: some fruits are small and sour, others large and sweet. The Russian botanist Nikolai Vavilov had already argued in the 1920s that this was where the apple came from.

Seeds and cuttings travelled west with traders and their horses along the routes of the Silk Road. On the way the Asian apple crossed with the European crab apple, which added genes to the modern fruit. The wild forests are now shrinking, and conservationists value them as a store of genes for disease resistance.
sum: In 2010 scientists published the complete genome of the apple. It confirmed that the wild apple of the Tian Shan mountains of Central Asia, Malus sieversii, is the main ancestor of the apples we eat.
